Anthropic could not be more different. It has generated strong revenue growth, but only in the short term, added to this, it is still unprofitable. Anthropic is another major tech company that requires investors to have a lot of faith about the future generation of revenues based on technology that will change the world. item.title: The unthinkable has come to pass: Tom Brady is a pretty good broadcaster
item.description: The former NFL quarterback was widely derided when he starter his job in the Fox booth. But he has shown a human side and explains the game beautifully I have accidentally force-fed myself Tom Brady’s commentary as my primary means of watching the NFL this season. When my favorite team, the Steelers, hired Mike McCarthy as head coach , I lodged a silent protest by declining to spend the several hundred dollars needed to get NFL Sunday Ticket. I didn’t even splurge for RedZone. That means I’ve found myself watching Fox’s NFL broadcasts on a Sunday – often an underwhelming Cowboys game – where Brady is the color commentator in the network’s No 1 booth, alongside play-by-play man Kevin Burkhardt. This two-and-a-half-month experiment has led me to an alarming conclusion, one I’d seen others reaching gradually over the last year but never taken too seriously myself. Recently, though, the truth has become unavoidable: Tom Brady is pretty good at his job. Gone are the days of the best quarter

item.title: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras
item.description: We can’t make AI safe for humanity if tech bosses are allowed to run their companies like autocracies Over the past two years, a troubling pattern has emerged across the world’s leading AI laboratories. Time and again, a safety researcher or engineer walks out of the door with a public warning that commercial pressures are overriding safety guardrails. Last month, the person who oversaw safety reports for OpenAI’s product releases said he was quitting the ChatGPT creator because the company’s culture was “broken” and the entire AI industry was too careless in developing the technology. The previous month it was a researcher at OpenAI’s rival Anthropic who quit, warning that he believed AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”. As a society we applaud the courage of these individuals and debate their warnings for a news cycle – and then we move on. But we miss the deeper institutional failure those resignations reveal: as the great political scientist Albert Hirschman made clear,

Suzanna is being raised by grandparents while her mother serves a life sentence for driving the getaway car for a botched bank robbery intended to fund revolutionary political activism. Although Suzanna refuses the narrative, in some ways this is a coming-of-age story, but with a protagonist whose overwhelming need is to go nowhere and change nothing. The Hill is shaped by the tension between the novel’s need for a plot and Suzanna’s rejection of her own role in the Bildungsroman. item.description: Much like tomato, the plum has a natural acidity and sweetness that works brilliantly in a delightfully jammy pasta sauce Standing on platform 2 at Baker Street station a few weeks ago, a grey creature scuttled under the raised tracks. “You’re never more than six feet away from a rat in London,” I said to my Roman son. “It’s a mouse, Mum,” was his hardboiled reply to my rehashing of an urban myth. A myth that turns out to be inaccurate, according to Dr David Cowan , whose research on the subject resulted in estimates of anything from 10ft-164ft: in other words, while it’s impossible to know for sure, in certain areas you might be very close to a rat. The same can be said about wild plum trees all over the world. While it’s impossible to know exactly, even in dense urban areas, you might be very close to a wild plum tree or, more correctly, a cultivated plum that has gone feral. item.title: Ram through datacentres no one wants and hope the AI bubble never bursts: that’s the UK’s growth plan | George Monbiot
item.description: The government doesn’t know what they are going to be used for, but that’s beside the point. Their real purpose is to sustain the share price of big tech It should have the status of an economic law: the sectors a government does most to promote in the name of growth are the sectors most likely to tank the economy. In the UK and the US, deregulation was meant to turn the financial sector into a never-ending growth machine. We have not yet fully recovered from the crash it helped cause in 2008. Fossil fuels are the most heavily subsidised sector on Earth. All that public money makes us highly vulnerable to oil price shocks, the whims of autocrats and societal collapse caused by climate breakdown. As for the great growth priority of our time – AI and datacentres – well, don’t take it from me. item.title: Nothing but highlights: is Power Slap the sport we deserve?
item.description: Slap fighting is the world’s newest combat sport. Built for short attention spans and super-viral moments, it’s aiming for global dominance. No flinching In the days before Power Slap 22, in Belgrade, Serbia, in late July, the organisers of the world’s newest combat sport were taking no chances. At the Crowne Plaza hotel, where competitors were booked to stay, those facing off had been separated by floor, lest any unauthorised violence took place. It turned out there was little need. The night before the main event, contestants mingled amiably in the lobby and bar. The atmosphere was more specialist sales conference than brewing barroom brawl. In the lobby, I joined Louis “Razor” Robinson, and Ryan “the Punisher” Kenny. “We’re all friends in slap,” Robinson said, earnestly, by way of a greeting. Robinson, a Brit from Stalybridge, Greater Manchester, is 30, stout, intense. Kenny, a Canadian, is 34, lofty, laid back. Continue reading...

item.title: Tricks! Traps! Riddles! Jan van Eyck’s portraits look vividly real – but are full of secret messages. What do they mean?
item.description: The more you gaze at ​these 10 surviving works, ​with their cryptic inscriptions and even fool’s gold, the more the Flemish master trips you up​ – but being laughed at like this is all part of the glorious pleasure Van Eyck: The Portraits review – a jewel box of phenomenal death-defeating paintings At the Barbican Art Gallery in London, there is an exhibition of some of the white paintings made by the US artist Robert Ryman over 60 years from the 1950s. The paintings are square, because a square is neutral, and he didn’t want viewers associating them with the visual language of landscape or portrait. For Ryman, his paintings resolutely were what they were, which is to say, white paint applied to various surfaces and fixed to the wall. Not “windows” through which one could glimpse another world. item.title: Andy Burnham is in danger of over-selling his big Brussels summit. What happens if he under-delivers? | Joël Reland
item.description: In laying a trap for himself, the PM could derail his longer-term ambition of revisiting Brexit This week’s UK-EU summit may, one day, be seen as the start of the UK’s long march back towards the EU. Andy Burnham’s much-anticipated first meeting with EU chiefs in Brussels on Friday will be used to unveil a suite of detailed agreements to improve trade and economic cooperation, before the Prime Minister kickstarts his longer term “national conversation” about a much closer form of political and economic relationship with the EU. This, as Burnham signalled in a speech on Monday night , could well culminate in Labour’s next election manifesto abandoning the party’s famous red lines, and proposing an application for EU membership. For pro-Europeans, this must read like a fever dream. Just four months ago, when Burnham took office, such a bold offer on Europe from the Labour party seemed implausible. item.title: ‘I came close to killing Sally about six times’: how my abusive father was enabled by his fame
item.description: Like Russell Brand, my father was put on a pedestal by the media, despite a history of troubling, misogynistic comments. Meanwhile, my mother suffered through years of appalling treatment Even though decades have passed, part of me feels I should not be telling this story. Not because it isn’t true, but because telling makes it real. And the reality is very hard to bear. I was a young child at home in Whitechapel, east London, when my mother came into my bedroom, which was next to my parents’, and told me that my father had raped her. He had gone off to work and I was too young to fully understand what the words meant – perhaps seven or eight – and I remember being angry with her for upsetting life again, as she had done before, when she suddenly came to me at the top of the stairs and told me that they would “have to part” and that would mean taking me away with her. Continue reading...

item.description: Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report. item.title: The Guardian view on the Trump, Xi and Putin meeting: it may be a first, but it’s not progress | Editorial
item.description: A trilateral gathering is good news for China and Russia, but bad for the US – and its traditional allies “Historic” is a neutral descriptor, not a favourable one. Things can be unprecedented for good reason. Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China on Thursday will be the first time that the leaders of the US, China and Russia have gathered for talks as a trio. The trilateral on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is striking, but it is not an achievement. The lack of a clear agenda is telling: the spectacle really is the substance. Mr Trump sees international affairs in terms of spheres of influence. This meeting reinforces the obvious conclusion for the rest of the world – that they don’t get to sit at the table, only to be on the plate. Mr Xi promotes the notion of a multipolar world. item.title: I jumped from a plane at 12,000ft. In mid-air, a friend’s knee collided into my neck
item.description: A group of eight trainee parachutists did the jump, and not far from the ground, disaster struck. Rob Bugden describes how he rebuilt his life after the accident that changed everything The skydive was going to plan. At 12,000ft, Rob Bugden jumped from the plane, quickly getting himself stable by arching his back to create a solid base. He checked for speed and altitude on his watch, and when he was low enough, pulled the parachute’s toggles. “I looked up. Good canopy.” But then: “Cut to black. And I’m waking up in a hospital in Phoenix.” It was 21 January 2016, the final day of his Royal Air Force high altitude training in the US, when 30-year-old Bugden collided – mid-air – with his friend, Brook Stebbings. They were moving into the landing stack formation, a vertical queue of eight parachutists flying in a holding pattern at different altitudes, when, at approximately 1,000ft, Stebbings’ knee crashed into him, breaking his neck. item.description: He seemed like the thinking person’s tech titan. But then came the affairs, the share collapse – and of course, the sorry items in his wardrobe A few years ago, I attended a small dinner at a friend’s house in the US at which a tech billionaire was the guest of honour. He wasn’t one of the most famous tech billionaires – I’d never heard of him, although I used his communications platform every day. Nonetheless, it was exciting to get up close to someone that staggeringly rich to see if he was different from the rest of us. And he was different, sort of. Leaning back in his chair, he seemed to suggest, in a bored kind of way, that in the event of a US standoff with Russia, Putin nuking London would be the sort of collateral damage Washington could tolerate. A bit of an odd thing to say to a stranger. He didn’t observe the usual rules of conversation but rather, like a Roman emperor waiting to be entertained, remained belligerently aloof. item.title: Twenty years ago, the Wii and PS3 predicted the future of gaming – did they get it right?
item.description: Both launched in 2006, with contrasting visions of gaming – one focused on accessibility, the other on technical ambition – each leaving a lasting legacy • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The main focus of the games industry this week is, of course, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI – a game that could define the next decade for the industry. For this week’s newsletter though, I wanted to direct your attention two decades into the past. In November 2006, two console manufacturers launched their competing – and wildly different – visions of what the future of video games would look like. Twenty years later, it’s clear that somehow they were both right. And yet, in some ways, they were both wrong. For Nintendo, the Wii was the natural extension of its famous maxim, Kareta Gijutsu no Suihei Shikō – roughly translated as lateral thinking with withered technology. item.title: A TikTok superstar bares all: Siorna Ashby’s best shot
item.description: Portraits often rely on the face and eyes to communicate. Here, I wanted to explore how much of Meg’s presence and personality could come through her body and gesture I met Meg at a nude life-drawing class. I was struck by how free she seemed and how powerfully that came through in her modelling. I asked if I could photograph her for my project Body Like Mine. This series explores the difference between how our bodies are perceived externally and how we experience them ourselves. We see a body and we bring our own judgments and assumptions on to it, but the lived experience is very different. Rather than portraying an idealised body, the project aims to explore what it feels like to inhabit your own body, and to see it as worthy of attention without asking it to become anything else first. Prof Peter Hindmarsh, a specialist in hormones in children, was crucial to the crown’s argument that the British nurse had poisoned children by injecting insulin into fluid bags. item.title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
item.description: With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. item.title: The Man Who Broke Reality by Philip Ball review – the inspirational genius of Niels Bohr
item.description: Scientific discoveries are explained effortlessly in this portrait of a man whose research was driven by pure passion Niels Bohr shares with Albert Einstein pride of place in the pantheon of 20th-century science. The two had much in common. They were not expert mathematicians; they prized physical intuition over mere competence; and they did not shy away from the moral and political implications of their work. But Bohr differed from Einstein in one crucial respect: his extraordinary personality. In his gripping biography Philip Ball ensures we feel the intense pull of Bohr’s genius. Today he would probably be considered neurodivergent; he possessed a passion for physics that cast a spell on all who knew him. Solving problems is the raison d’etre of any scientist, but Bohr went far beyond that: having inaugurated quantum mechanics with his model of the atom in 1913, he simply would not give up until the rest of it was understood. Continue reading...

item.title: ‘They want silence’: how the film NAZA is shaking Israel

item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03777-7 Teeth found in south China challenge the idea that Homo erectus was limited to woodlands and savannahs.

item.title: Intra-stellar: a star inside a giant star
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03273-y Long-term monitoring of a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy reveals, for the first time, the decay of the orbit of another star inside the giant’s envelope.

item.title: Glucose-powered implant brings devices for treating diabetes a step closer
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03377-5 A device that stimulates the main nerve between the brain and the internal organs when blood sugar is high is an effective therapy in rat models of diabetes.

item.title: Band-Edge-Extended Heterointerfaces for Perovskite Solar Cells and Tandems
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11427-1 Band-Edge-Extended Heterointerfaces for Perovskite Solar Cells and Tandems

item.title: Poxviruses probably evolved in the digestive system of animals
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03436-x Large and giant DNA viruses that infect unicellular eukaryotes are abundant in the environment but have rarely been found in the gut microbiome. The discovery of such viruses that prevail in the digestive system of humans and animals exposes a long-overlooked facet of the gut microbiome that clarifies the origin of poxviruses.

item.title: Meet ‘egoviruses’: the surprise microbes living in the guts of millions of people
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03766-w Egoviruses could be the evolutionary missing link between giant viruses that infect single-celled organisms and those that can infect people.

item.title: A new view of Amazonian leaf seasonality
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03490-5 Much of the Amazon rainforest was thought to be evergreen, but high-resolution satellite imagery reveals that many of its trees can remain leafless for longer than expected.

item.title: Injured locusts heal or are cannibalized depending on levels of a bacterial odour molecule
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03599-7 When migratory locusts are injured, an odorous chemical produced by bacteria living in or on their bodies activates the immune system, helping them to fight disease-causing agents. However, when a wound is large and the chemical becomes too concentrated, it attracts cannibalistic locusts.

item.title: Are you a budding science sleuth? Take our plagiarism quiz to test your skills
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03040-z Sleuths and publishers seize on ‘tortured phrases’ to detect research fraud. Sometimes they can raise a smile.

item.title: AI must be held accountable — value statements won’t protect human dignity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03717-5 Technology companies can’t be the judges of their own regulatory compliance. Centuries of history explain why.

item.title: A grant to hand out more grants — and build a research area
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03689-6 A rapid microgrants scheme called the Field Building Accelerator aims to launch new scientific fields.

item.title: Quantum physics can prove where you are
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03378-4 Demonstrating your location to someone far away is surprisingly hard. Quantum correlations offer a way to do so without needing to trust any quantum hardware.

item.title: The right to do wrong
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03517-x An equal chance.

item.title: Widespread deciduousness reveals diverse Amazonian phenological strategies
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11284-y A basin-wide assessment of Amazonian deciduousness using high-resolution satellite observations shows a diverse range of phenological strategies across the Amazon rainforest, contrary to the prevailing view of Amazonian phenology.

item.title: Observation of tunable superradiant frequency combs
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11289-7 A transition from continuous to periodic pulsed superradiant emission in coupled spin–resonator systems is demonstrated, revealing connections to time crystals and enabling synchronized microwave and optical frequency combs.

item.title: Rethinking corporate climate targets for real-world transitions
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11100-7 Frameworks for corporate greenhouse gas reduction targets should place greater emphasis on systemic changes in business models, technologies and value chains; the scientific community has a role in developing robust, actionable frameworks for corporate decarbonization.

item.title: Analogue simulation of massive relativistic quantum fields in 2 + 1 dimensions
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11268-y Analogue simulation of massive relativistic quantum fields in 2 + 1 dimensions (two spatial dimensions and time) is realized using two coherently coupled spin components in a two-dimensional atomic Bose–Einstein condensate.

item.title: A glucose-powered artificial neuroimmune axis for metabolic control
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11251-7 NeuroAxis restores glucose tolerance, improves insulin sensitivity and normalizes glycaemic control, with therapeutic effects persisting after treatment cessation in rat models of type 1 and type 2 diabetes.

item.title: Conservation of the tumour microenvironment across organs and species
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11270-4 A pan-cancer single-cell analysis of the tumour microenvironment across 42 cancer types and across 2 species is described.

item.title: Quantum position verification with remote untrusted devices
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11247-3 A loophole-free Bell-test quantum protocol demonstrates secure, device-independent position verification, achieving up to 4.53-fold smaller localization volumes than classical methods and enabling tamper-resistant location-based authentication.

item.title: Quantum resistance paradox of low-dimensional superfluids
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11294-w A defect-free unitary Fermi gas is used in a digitally programmable transport geometry to isolate geometric effects on superfluid dissipation and discover a paradox.

item.title: Fully integrated perovskite active polaritonic circuits
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11299-5 A fully integrated perovskite polaritonic circuit that brings the functionalities of fully integrated on-chip polaritonic systems simultaneously delivering room-temperature waveguide lasing, controllable optical routing and amplification together in a single-step-grown platform is shown.

item.title: TransA-MERFISH reveals divergent post-retinal direction-selective circuits
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11235-7 TransA-MERFISH combines anterograde trans-neuronal tracing and spatial transcriptomics and reveals distinct retinal on–off direction-selective ganglion cell-dependent and independent motion-selective pathways in superior colliculus, establishing a sensitive cell-type-resolved framework for wiring-diagram reconstruction in early visual processing.

item.title: Flat-band-induced integer doping and phase transition in monolayer graphene
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11254-4 An architecture comprising monolayer graphene doubly aligned to bulk and monolayer hBN on either side shows a gate-tunable global structural phase transition between two stacking configurations, accompanied by flat-band-induced integer doping.

item.title: Rainforest adaptation in late Homo erectus from southern China
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11155-6 Eight Homo erectus teeth from two caves in southern China reveal that the species persisted in closed rainforest ecosystems between 324 and 184 ka, challenging assumptions about their ecological preferences and behavioural limitations.

item.title: Bogong moths navigate with a light-dependent geomagnetic inclination compass
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11322-9 During their biannual migration, nocturnal Bogong moths (Agrotis infusa) rely on both a stellar and a geomagnetic compass for navigation, enabling them to maintain their migratory direction even if one of these cues is missing.

item.title: An inspiral of a star inside a common envelope with its giant companion
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11221-z Observations of AT 2025abao provide direct evidence of common-envelope inspiral, revealing frictional energy dissipation and constraining how orbital energy drives stellar-envelope ejection during binary evolution.

item.title: Global patterns and drivers of bee richness and endemism on islands
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11325-6 Gobal analysis of bee species across 305 islands reveals that islands account for 20% of global bee diversity, with more than 4,100 species and high levels of endemism, and shows that richness is shaped by island size, isolation and evolutionary diversification.

item.title: Host–microbe interactions in engineered immunocompetent human gut tissues
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11292-y Engineered barrier models of the small intestine and colon that include immune cells and a microbial compartment enable characterizations of the human epithelial response to Salmonella Typhimurium at the single-cell level.

item.title: Injury-induced signalling coordinates immunity and cannibalism in locusts
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11297-7 Studies in migratory locusts identify a dual role of volatile guaiacol emission, enhancing survival of individual insects following minor injury but attracting cannibalistic attack once an injury severity threshold has been exceeded.

item.title: Structural and regulatory evolution across the genus Hordeum
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11332-7 Chromosome-scale pangenomics across diploid Hordeum species reveals extensive structural variation, hybridization, introgression, horizontal gene transfer and regulatory evolution, revealing adaptive trait diversification and providing genomic resources for barley improvement.

item.title: Evidence for late Middle Pleistocene Homo erectus in mainland East Asia
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11271-3 Late Middle Pleistocene hominin teeth from the Naxian and Baxian caves of southern China, dated to around 324–184 thousand years ago, fill a gap in the geographical and chronological distribution of Homo erectus in East Asia.

item.title: Closest relatives of poxviruses prevail in human and animal guts worldwide
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11283-z A diversified group of DNA viruses with large linear genomes is discovered, egoviruses, that comprise a putative viral order most closely related to animal-infecting poxviruses, and prevail in the animal digestive system.

item.title: Evidence for p-wave magnetism in electronic band structure of metallic EuSi
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11295-9 A combination of symmetry analysis, first-principles calculations, neutron scattering and photoemission spectroscopy shows p-wave magnetism in the near-Fermi-level electronic structure of stoichiometric metallic EuSi.

item.title: Designing dislocation-driven polar vortex networks in twisted perovskites
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11330-9 Experimental and theoretical investigation of twisted freestanding SrTiO3 layers using various analytic methods from 4DSTEM to DFT reveal a long-range ordered screw dislocation pattern as well as topological polar vortex arrays in the interface plane.

item.title: Transient contacts between filaments impart its elasticity to branched actin
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11300-1 Stiffness of branched actin networks emerges from the formation of contacts between filaments, with growth under load resulting in stiffer networks.

item.title: Tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11298-6 Tropical land-use intensification drives substantial biodiversity loss and reorganizes community composition, with aboveground assemblages showing an increase in nestedness in monocultures compared with forests, underscoring the need for landscape-scale, multi-taxon conservation that integrates agricultural and natural habitats.

item.title: Ferroptosis in cancer cells triggers PGE<sub>2</sub> production for tumour immune escape
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11333-6 Ferroptotic cancer cells activate a molecular program that causes increased levels of PGE2, which in turn impairs type 1 conventional dendritic cell function, compromising antitumour CD8+ T cell immunity.

item.title: Hypothalamic volume and cell-type changes in ageing and Alzheimer’s disease
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11305-w HypoAD, an atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and Alzheimer’s disease that combines high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging from 458 individuals with single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 614,403 nuclei, reveals that metabolism- and circadian-regulating subregions, and their inhibitory neurons and microglia, are particularly vulnerable.

item.description: At a potentially critical juncture for football, the PFA’s chief executive talks about the organisation, wider fears in the game and why the Folarin Balogun affair was ‘scandalous’ After five years in charge of the Professional Footballers’ Association, what has Maheta Molango learned? “The game is in danger,” the 44-year-old says. “I’ve learned that the game I loved and led me to first play and then advise and then lead a club and today to lead the PFA, is in danger because it is being forgotten.” In 2026, with football ubiquitous on all platforms, with a World Cup that generated $15bn (£11.4bn) in revenue, and with attendances across the English pyramid growing year on year, it may seem hard to imagine forgetting about the game. But Molango’s unique perspective as head of the players’ union for England and Wales observes a different picture; one where the future of the sport is being determined not by what will maintain its popularity, but what will make the most money. item.title: The Guardian view on climate and debt: a vicious cycle the world must break at Cop31 | Editorial
item.description: Poor countries are paying creditors instead of preparing for climate disasters. The international financial system must stop deepening their vulnerability The catastrophe that struck Nepal’s Himalayas in August began with a collapsing glacier. An avalanche of ice and rock unleashed deadly floods, sweeping away villages, bridges and roads, and leaving thousands dead or missing. It illustrated the dangers posed by global heating to the Himalayas’ increasingly unstable glaciers. Nepal lost a tenth of its electricity generation. Reconstruction will cost about $5bn. Yet the Loss and Damage Fund, hailed as a historic breakthrough at the 2022 UN climate summit, has earmarked just $20m for Nepal – less than 5% of the $482m that Kathmandu must pay its external public creditors this year. “The scale of resources needs to increase,” Nepal’s delegation to this year’s UN climate conference drily observed. They are not the only ones agitating for change at Cop31. In its September report, Debt Fuels

item.title: Keepsake County review – eccentric stealing simulator with a social conscience
item.description: PC; Forward Instinct This irreverent stealth game depicts Samuel’s lonely life robbing garish, midwestern abodes – it’s a Shameless way to make a living For many people, McMansions are an eyesore, but for the protagonist of Keepsake County, a renowned burglar, they are an enticing opportunity. Prowling at purple-hued dusk, this unfussy thief is just as likely to steal a half-eaten slice of pizza or a naff ceramic ornament as he is an expensive set of golf clubs. It’s a sad, desperate way to make a living, a sense compounded by what this fledgling kleptomaniac carries his loot away in: a plastic shopping bag. Countless works have taken us to breadline America, from classic novel East of Eden to acclaimed TV crime drama Mare of Easttown. But Keepsake County is no prestige examination of the economic underbelly of the US. item.title: Help! Why does my apple pie always have a soggy base? | Kitchen aide
item.description: Direct the heat and minimise the moisture to save your pastry from a saturated bottom, says our panel of pie pros Why does the pastry base of my apple pie always come out soggy? What am I doing wrong? Sophie, by email “The very first thing I would say is that Sophie has got to look at her filling, and how wet it is,” says Calum Franklin, author of The Modern Pie Maker and all-round pie Yoda. “Apples contain quite a lot of water already, so you don’t generally need to add any extra liquid to the filling.” Instead, he’d simply cook the apples with sugar: “Just let them break down.” That said, Sophie could always consider including some sort of barrier, too, says Dee Rettali, co-founder of Fortitude Bakehouse in London: “My mother was an amazing baker, and she always sprinkled a very fine crumble mix [just sugar and flour, no fat] on the bottom of her pie before putting in any fruit. That will then absorb most of the liquid.” Got a culinary dilemma? Email feast@theguardian.com Continue re

item.title: They’re one of the UK’s greatest cult bands – who swore they’d never reunite. What brought Life Without Buildings back together?
item.description: The Scottish quartet existed for just three years at the turn of the millennium. But after Frank Ocean and TikTok thrilled to Sue Tompkins’ unique vocals, they’re back. They explain their fears about ‘spoiling the joy’ ‘I’m excited, I’m scared, I’m anxious – that bubbling feeling, like when you’re on a rollercoaster, at the very top, just before the big drop.” On a drizzly afternoon in July, huddled with her three bandmates in the cramped cupboard that’s the dressing room of Glasgow venue Mono, Sue Tompkins is managing her feelings ahead of her first proper gig with Life Without Buildings in almost a quarter of a century. “Everybody coming is invited, it’s secret, nobody paid much to get in, the profits are going to charity,” adds guitarist Robert Dallas Gray, sat beside her, as much to steady his own nerves as to explain the circumstances of tonight’s show. “I hope people aren’t looking at it like we’re fucking entertainers .” Continue reading...

item.title: Janine van Wyk: ‘Our rooms were empty … no mattresses, no lightbulbs and not a drop of water’
item.description: In an extract from the former South Africa captain’s book, she details less than ideal Wafcon 2006 preparations I was just a year into my international career when we qualified for my first Wafcon, which was then called the African Women’s Championship (AWC) and was held in Nigeria in 2006. I was extremely excited but very nervous to participate in this tournament, more so when it was announced that we would be in the same group as the hosts, and would play them last in the group. As it turned out, it would be the game that decided who finished top of the group. By then we had beaten Algeria 4-0 and Equatorial Guinea 2-0 and had to travel to Delta State to take on the hosts. I’d heard that Nigeria was the toughest country to travel to and I was about to realise why. It’s become common knowledge that South Africans and Nigerians are massive rivals on the football field but also don’t really get on off it. Continue reading...

It is a life that spans the extremes of privilege and distress, and half a century of seismic national history. Yet when the chance came, the deal with the country’s biggest publisher, Penguin Random House India, fell through at the last minute over what it termed “an impasse over a particular issue” in the text, with HarperCollins stepping into the breach. He’s always asking what more we can do.” Four years on from that unexpected email, Fiesser was given the secret task of reaching out for a letter for Saka to read from the podium when he was presented with the Sócrates award at last month’s Ballon d’Or ceremony in London for his humanitarian work. He finished with three centre-backs on the pitch. His team could not get out of their half in the final part of the game. So close your eyes and imagine an alternate universe in which James Trafford did not make his stunning double save in stoppage time on Sunday and England had drawn 3-3 with Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium rather than won 3-2 . The reaction would not have been kind because Tuchel has been here before. The head coach wanted to push one particular comparison from the World Cup over the summer. “It was Mexico reloaded,” he said, with a nod towards the 3-2 last-16 win at the Azteca Stadium and it fitted like a glove – down to the detail of Jarell Quansah and red cards. item.description: As tourism booms, three experienced female travellers give their take on how to make the most of travelling here • Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to India. But he catalogued it in his famous work The Wonders of Creation and Rarities of Existence, which drew on accounts of a distant land filled with “rarities par excellence”. For al-Qazwini, as Helen Pfeifer writes in the London Review of Books, wonder was not an emotion but an intellectual method of making sense of the world and acquiring knowledge. India has long occupied such a space in the global imagination, as a land of extraordinary riches; spirituality, customs, chaos and contradictions. This has shaped how the country is perceived from afar, but it can often flatten its complexities. Continue reading...

item.title: The Brightness by Chad Harbach review – an ambitious sequel to The Art of Fielding
item.description: Fifteen years on, this expansive follow-up to the campus epic explores female agency, friendship – and the messiness of early adulthood Back in 2011, Chad Harbach’s debut The Art of Fielding was hailed as the next Great American Novel. Set on the campus of Westish, a fictional midwestern liberal arts college, and steeped in baseball, it grappled with the big, quintessentially American themes – ambition, failure, the pursuit of perfection – that have traditionally been the genre’s hallmark. Harbach himself winkingly invited the categorisation: The Art of Fielding communes directly with the spirit of Herman Melville, arguably the greatest Great American Novelist of them all. Westish College, the novel explains, has claimed Melville as its own since the discovery of a lecture he gave there in 1880: its baseball team is known as the Harpooners; and a Melville statue presides over the campus like the genius of the place. item.title: The root-to-tip revolution! An A-Z of how to eat plants in full – for extra flavour, fibre and savings
item.description: If you discard the peels, skins, stalks and seeds when consuming fruit and vegetables you are missing out on a lot of value. Here’s what to incorporate into your diet – and what to avoid Do you peel your potatoes, deseed your squash and core your cauliflower? A study by King’s College London , published last month in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition , found that people who routinely discard peels, skins, stalks and seeds when preparing fruit and vegetables are missing out on a valuable source of dietary fibre. Ten out of the 12 types of produce the researchers analysed had higher levels of fibre in the scraps than in the flesh. Eating these often overlooked parts could help address the global dietary fibre deficit and tackle food waste, they say. Here, experts share their advice on how to cook and eat “root to tip”. item.title: A material just one atom thick reveals a strange quantum secret
item.description: Researchers at the University of Osaka have discovered a remarkable quantum state forming at the boundary between a one-atom-thick material and a metal. item.description: Deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have discovered tiny hidden ecosystems inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form. item.title: The pet I’ll never forget: Mr Baxter, who ate our belongings – and broke our hearts
item.description: Reared on a puppy farm, and abandoned by a previous owner, he was half-starved when we adopted him. But he grew strong, chomping through everything from dog beds to sunglasses and my debut book The day we brought our 14-week-old cocker spaniel home in 2022, I was wearing a silk scarf I’d picked up decades ago in a vintage shop in Tokyo. I didn’t know it then but that rainy afternoon would be the last time I’d wear it. Three days later, it was in my new puppy’s mouth. Once he’d finished tearing my scarf to shreds, he gazed at me with soulful chocolate brown eyes, fluttering his long eyelashes. No matter how fond I was of that silk scarf, how could I be angry? Puppies chew stuff. That’s what they do. Mr Baxter gnawed his way through four dog beds, blankets and multiple dog leads. Nothing was off-limits. item.title: A 19-year study reveals a troubling link between napping and death
item.description: A surprising new study suggests that when and how often older adults nap could reveal hidden warning signs about their health. Researchers followed 1,338 people for up to 19 years and discovered that longer, more frequent naps were linked to higher mortality, while morning nappers faced a 30% greater risk of death than afternoon nappers. Each additional hour of daytime sleep was associated with a 13% increase in mortality risk.

Developed by University of Texas researchers, the device uses gentle ultrasound to stimulate deep brain regions, helping participants enter REM sleep 43 minutes faster and remain there 16 minutes longer on average. The technology also showed promising effects on stress regulation and brain circuits involved in emotion.

item.description: Lapwood/Nidaros Cathedral Girls’ Choir (Sony) Lapwood has turned Howard Shore’s film score into an impressive full-blown organ symphony When a fan requested she play Concerning Hobbits from The Lord of the Rings, little did Anna Lapwood imagine that she would go on to spend a year turning Howard Shore’s leitmotif-led soundtrack into a full-blown organ symphony. Remarkably, she transcribed all but one segment by ear, a feat in itself. That she manages to tell the story chronologically over a 38-minute, three-movement span is equally impressive. But wait, there’s more. Reckoning the symphony would benefit from the human voice, she incorporated a handful of songs, performing them live – in Tolkien’s Elvish dialect – while playing the Nidaros Cathedral organ in Trondheim, Norway. item.title: An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different
item.description: A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago may have helped shape one of the most important differences between humans and our closest relatives: how our brains develop. Scientists at Lund University discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene called LINC00662, which remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in early brain development.

item.title: Uranus and Neptune’s bizarre magnetic fields may finally be explained
item.description: The strange, wildly tilted magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune have puzzled scientists since NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft explored the planets in the 1980s. New simulations suggest that extreme conditions deep inside these icy giants create unusual electrical properties that could explain their magnetic fields. Remarkably, the models indicate that their magnetic poles could shift by tens of degrees within just a few decades, far faster than Earth's.

item.title: A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections
item.description: A surprising discovery from Rockefeller University suggests that a common amino acid could play a powerful role in protecting against cancer and viral infections. Scientists found that low arginine levels interfere with the immune system's ability to recognize dangerous cells, while increasing arginine intake reduced colon cancer tumors and improved viral infection outcomes in mice. Even more remarkably, giving mice arginine after they contracted influenza helped them recover.

item.title: The unexpected power of fleeting friendships
item.description: From Aristotle on, we’ve learned to see long-lasting relationships as more valuable. But what does that leave out? In Russian, a poputchik is a stranger you meet on a journey who you end up confessing everything to because you know you’ll never see them again. Like the English “fellow traveller”, poputchik was repurposed to describe Marxist sympathisers, but the original meaning intrigues me most. The idea that we might safely unburden ourselves to strangers, or have their secrets bestowed upon us, is deeply embedded in Russian culture. It’s there in Leo Tolstoy’s The Kreutzer Sonata: as the windows tremble and the tundra passes in a hypnotic blur, Pozdnyshev tells his life story of marriage, betrayal and murder. Or in Venedikt Erofeev’s 1970s satire Moscow to the End of the Line , in which a retired cable fitter drunkenly hops a train and unfurls a sublime monologue on politics, society, love and, of course, vodka. A Russian friend jokes that this is “therapy, Soviet-style”. Continue

item.title: Terry Butcher: ‘I’ve learned to live with the Hand of God goal better’
item.description: The former England centre-back answers your questions on Diego Maradona, Bobby Robson and on staying in strange places “Have you made up all these on your own?” asks Terry Butcher, sitting in a London office in the week he is presented with his England legacy cap. It turns out dozens of Guardian readers want to pick the brains of a much-loved centre-back who was feted en route to a World Cup semi-final and tormented four years previously by the mercurial genius of Diego Maradona. Did Maradona ever admit to the “Hand of God”? Butcher found himself in the post-match doping-control room alongside his nemesis at the Azteca in 1986. “I tapped my head, then my hand, and then he tapped his head,” Butcher says. “He didn’t admit to it because, if he had, I’d have been right across that room.” Continue reading...

item.title: I’m really hurt that my parents didn’t give me a 40th birthday gift | Ask Annalisa Barbieri
item.description: You feel overlooked, but your parents’ disappointing behaviour does not necessarily mean they don’t love you I turned 40 a few years ago . For my 21st and 30th birthdays I got jewellery from my parents, so when they didn’t ask what I wanted, I assumed they would follow this tradition. But I got nothing. Not even an apology. It later transpired that they thought I was turning 41. But even then to receive nothing is hurtful . They blamed it on old age and said they had been struggling with their health. I place a lot of importance on gift giving . It isn’t about the value, but it’s nice to feel someone has spent time thinking about you . To get nothing just screamed that they didn’t care. Continue reading...

item.title: Alzheimer’s may start shrinking two brain regions years before memory loss
item.description: Johns Hopkins scientists have uncovered hidden warning signs of Alzheimer’s disease that may appear up to a decade before memory loss begins. Brain scans revealed that two regions involved in memory and emotion start shrinking before the hippocampus, the area doctors typically examine for signs of Alzheimer’s. These early changes are linked to abnormal tau protein buildup and could provide a powerful new way to identify people at risk.

item.title: Scientists discover a bizarre paradox among endangered penguins
item.description: A groundbreaking drone survey has revealed a startling split in the fate of New Zealand's endangered Erect-crested penguins. While one population has remained stable for decades, another has declined by more than 40%, apparently due to a combination of predators, worsening storms, and changing ocean conditions. Even more surprisingly, the tiny Bounty Islands support nearly as many breeding pairs as the Antipodes Islands, despite being 40 times smaller.

item.title: Dinosaurs may have been eating seaweed 100 million years ago
item.description: Dinosaurs may have been snacking on seaweed and other ocean foods more than 100 million years ago, according to surprising new evidence hidden in their fossilized teeth. Researchers discovered chemical signatures suggesting that coastal dinosaurs and other prehistoric animals relied partly on nutrients originating in the sea. The findings reveal that marine resources traveled through ancient food chains, supplementing the diets of everything from plant-eating dinosaurs to predators.

item.title: Physicists use laser light to unlock a crystal's hidden electrical powers
item.description: Scientists have discovered how to use flashes of laser light to organize tiny electrical regions inside a crystal, solving a decades-old mystery about how the material behaves. The laser-induced alignment lasts just a trillionth of a second, but the breakthrough could open the door to new ways of processing and storing information.

item.title: Euclid discovers ancient cosmic beacons from the dawn of time, shining like a trillion suns
item.description: ESA’s Euclid space telescope has discovered 31 ancient quasars, including two record-breaking objects that shone with the brightness of a trillion Suns when the Universe was just 670 million years old. Powered by supermassive black holes, these extraordinary cosmic beacons reveal a time when the first galaxies were still taking shape.

item.title: ‘You have to cope’: why don’t we hear of the ‘epidemic’ of women’s loneliness?
item.description: The world has become accustomed to concerns about the male loneliness epidemic. item.title: Scientists find a simple daily routine linked to less pain and depression
item.description: A simple change to your daily routine could make a surprising difference in how you feel, both physically and mentally. University of Missouri researchers found that older adults who followed consistent daily schedules reported less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they struggled with insomnia. Keeping regular times for sleeping, eating, and other activities may help regulate the body's internal clock, which influences mood, sleep, and overall health.

item.title: A new fiber supplement could help millions suffering from irritable bowel syndrome
item.description: Scientists have developed a promising new fiber supplement that improves gut health in people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) without worsening bloating, pain, or other digestive symptoms. The specially designed blend also improved gut-related anxiety and produced surprisingly rapid changes in gut bacteria, potentially offering a new way to manage IBS.

item.title: Stanford scientists discover hidden brain signals that predict Alzheimer’s years before symptoms
item.description: Stanford researchers have discovered that hidden patterns of brain activity can predict Alzheimer’s risk years before memory problems appear, potentially offering an earlier warning than traditional biomarkers. The same patterns also reveal which brains are unusually resistant to aging, raising hopes for future treatments that could help protect memory.

item.title: Exercise after ACL surgery may protect knees from early osteoarthritis
item.description: A new study suggests that the right kind of exercise could help protect young adults from early knee osteoarthritis following ACL surgery. Researchers found that a four-month supervised rehabilitation program improved pain, muscle strength, and quality of life without damaging knee cartilage. The findings challenge fears that exercise worsens injured knees and could transform how patients recover from ACL reconstruction.

item.title: 5,000-year-old skulls reveal a disturbing secret of ancient Egypt's first kings
item.description: A 5,000-year-old mystery surrounding the tombs of Egypt’s first kings has taken a disturbing turn. Scientists reexamining 46 ancient skulls discovered evidence of potentially fatal head injuries in 18, suggesting that at least 39% of those studied may have been deliberately killed. The findings support a century-old theory that royal attendants were sacrificed when kings died, possibly to serve them in the afterlife.

item.title: Forcing yourself to smile can actually make you miserable

In a University of Florida study involving more than 1,100 participants, researchers discovered that while a single artificial smile can provide a small mood boost, repeatedly faking smiles can erase that benefit or even reverse it.

item.title: Ultimate 1-50: the male footballers best associated with each squad number
item.description: Who is football’s most legendary No 9? Has there ever been a legendary No 28? And why exactly does Mario Balotelli love wearing No 45 so much? Here’s our list and the stories behind it The relationship between players and numbers is a long-established one filled with memories and fascinating as well as fun stories behind them. With that in mind, the Guardian has had a go at deciding which male player is best associated with each squad number, from 1-50. Various factors were taken into consideration, including how long a player wore/has worn that number, what they achieved/have achieved in it, why they decided to wear it in the first place and, in some cases, how distinctly it has become associated with them in death. The below list is highly subjective and ultimately a bit of fun, but don’t let that stop you being shocked and furious in equal measure. *** Continue reading...

item.title: Football comes together across Spain to honour Jesús de Miguel: ‘We’ve seen how fragile life is’
item.description: Across La Liga and beyond this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them In the final few minutes before stepping into the arena once more, heading out for his 199th Osasuna match on Saturday evening, the man who has scored more first division goals than anyone in their history stopped his teammates for a moment and told them what it meant to wear the shirt. “This is very important,” Ante Budimir began as the dressing room, their sanctuary, fell silent around him. “We don’t have this shirt today for the sake of it. He was not chosen, and nor are we. It could have happened to anyone, anyone. Let us go knowing that we’re grateful to be on the pitch: playing, watching, warming up, sitting on the bench, whatever it may be. Boys, we were not chosen: not us, not him. Let us go, gratefully. Without thought. We have a grand day before us.” With that, Osasuna’s players turned left out of the room, where they were joined in the tunnel by footballers from Athletic Clu

item.title: Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action
item.description: Delap’s talents resurface in style, Gómez delights Brighton with more fireworks, and hair-pulling confusion at Everton It would have been very easy for Oliver Glasner to lose patience with Liam Delap. The forward is still only 23, yet the days when he was rattling in 12 in a Premier League season for Ipswich have come to seem a very long time ago (and his six games for Manchester City even longer). A season at Chelsea had left him bereft of confidence, an odd mix of diffidence and overaggression, devoid of composure in the box, arms flailing like a broken windmill. But the old gifts have not left him. Both goals on Saturday were the result of great muscular surges and if the first finish seemed essentially about hitting the ball as hard as possible on target, the second was a precise – and still powerful – finish in off the far post. After games such as this it’s possible to imagine him as England’s long-term replacement for Harry Kane. Jonathan Wilson Match report: Nottingham Forest 3

item.title: Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top
item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure. Continue reading...
